catalog_quote: [p. 2] However, preliminary observations show influences from Aslian in terms of phonology, namely a strong word final accent (Pok, 2017) and some sesquisyllables (Tan, 2020). [...] [p. 40] I suspect this might have something to do with word stress or prominence, but due to time constraints, the present study will not cover suprasegmental features. [...] [p. 43] It has been observed that some words in Seletar have variant pronunciations involving “unstable” or “uncertain” vowels. The vowels involved in this variation usually are in the penultimate syllable, which is unstressed. Examples of this includeː ekat ‘to tie’ is mostly [ekat], but sometimes [ikat]; ekot ‘to follow’ is commonly [ekot], but [ikot] also occurs [...] [p. 45] With further analysis of Seletar narrative texts, the most noticeable ‘syllable and a half’ structure occurs in one word /ncak/ [n̩caʔ] ‘NEG’, which has a nasal serving as the nucleus of the first syllable (minor syllable). The stress falls on the second (major) syllable. [...] The minor syllable [n] for [n̩caʔ] has approximate duration of 0.08s, while the major syllable is 0.3s. [...] [p. 143] Past studies have noted that Seletar words have a strong word final accent, but research investigating the stress and rhythmic patterns of longer segments and texts is lacking.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Checked (263 pp., the PDF's metadata OK, title page 'A Sketch Grammar of Seletar / Tan Zhi Xuan / School of Humanities / 2022', MA thesis NTU) and its extracted text dump. Every quoted passage is present at the stated locator: printed p. 43 = p. 56 ('The vowels involved in this variation usually are in the penultimate[fn 55] syllable, which is unstressed.'; same page also 'The unstressed vowels in Maniq display more phonetic variation compared to the stressed final syllable vowel' as the explicit parallel); printed p. 45 = p. 58 ('..one word /ncak/ [n̩caʔ] NEG, which has a nasal serving as the nucleus of the first syllable (minor syllable). The stress falls on the second (major) syllable.'…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the final (ultimate) syllable of the word: the penultimate syllable is described as unstressed and its vowel unstable, the major (second) syllable of a sesquisyllabic word carries the stress, and earlier fieldworkers (Pok 2017; Juma'at 2017) report a strong word-final accent. Word-final vowels are frequently closed by a glottal stop, especially at the end of an intonational phrase or under stress (p. 41).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. The author explicitly says (p. 40) 'the present study will not cover suprasegmental features' and (p. 143) that the stress and rhythmic patterns of Seletar remain to be investigated; the word-final glottal closure is irregular in connected speech and tied to intonational-phrase ends.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (disyllabic and sesquisyllabic words from elicited wordlists and four natural texts, Kampung Sungai Temon and Kampung Bakar Batu, Johor Bahru); phrase-level remarks: glottal stop marks the end of an intonational phrase (pp. 38-40) and imperative clauses carry 'a heavy stress at the end of the clause' (p. 109). Author notes Seletar 'lacks a distinct iambic pattern' typical of Aslian sesquisyllabic languages (p. 45).
new_statements.identity_note: Tan 2022 describes Seletar (Bahasa Seletar / cap kon) of the Orang Seletar villages Kampung Sungai Temon and Kampung Bakar Batu, Johor Bahru, Malaysia = oran1259 [ors]; treated as a Malay dialect (>90% lexical similarity) with Aslian-like word-final accent. The earlier scan's named source 'McDowell & Anderbeck 2020, The Malay Lects of the Southern Malay Peninsula' is, per Glottolog ref 585807, actually titled 'The Malay Lects of Southern Sumatra'; the peninsula survey is Anderbeck 2016 (unpublished workshop paper).

sources.note: Ch. 5 Phonology (pp. 33-52) has no stress subsection and the author states (p. 40) that suprasegmental features are not covered; but it says first-hand that the penultimate syllable 'is unstressed' (p. 43), that in the sesquisyllable /n̩cak/ 'the stress falls on the second (major) syllable' (p. 45), that many words end 'with a heavy strong accent' closed by a glottal stop at the end of an intonational phrase or when stressed (p. 41), that imperative clauses carry 'a heavy stress at the end of the clause' (p. 109), and reports second-hand (pp. 2, 11, 143) a 'strong word final accent' from Pok…
